# Docker Container Restart Policies

One of Docker’s powerful features is the ability to **automatically restart containers** if they stop or crash unexpectedly. This built-in fault tolerance provides **basic self-healing** for containerized workloads—no external orchestration required.

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/refs/heads/main/Docker%20Labs/Lab%2004/images/image.png)

In this lab, you’ll learn all about Docker's **restart policies**, which are essential for maintaining uptime in containerized applications. You’ll explore how these policies behave, how they differ, and see them in action with hands-on demonstrations.

## Lab Overview

In this lab, you will:

- Understand the role of restart policies in Docker.
- Learn about the three major restart policies:
  - `always`
  - `unless-stopped`
  - `on-failure`
- Perform practical exercises to:
  - Launch containers with each policy.
  - Trigger restarts.
  - Observe Docker's behavior.
  - Restart the Docker daemon to test persistence.

By the end of this lab, you'll have a solid understanding of how to make your containers more resilient using restart policies.

## Concepts and Background

### What Are Restart Policies?

Restart policies are instructions given to the Docker engine about **how to react** when a container stops. They determine **if** and **when** the container should be restarted.

These are configured **per container** using:

- The `--restart` flag in `docker run`
- Or declaratively in tools like **Docker Compose**, **Swarm**, or **Kubernetes**

### Types of Restart Policies

| Policy          | Description                                                                                 |
|-----------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `always`        | Restart the container **no matter what**, even if it exits cleanly (exit code `0`).         |
| `unless-stopped`| Same as `always`, **except** it won't restart if the container was **manually stopped**.   |
| `on-failure`    | Restart only when the container **exits with a non-zero exit code** (i.e., it failed).      |

## Restart Policy: `always`

This policy will **restart the container no matter how it stops**, unless you manually remove it. Even after a Docker daemon restart, the container will come back up.

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/refs/heads/main/Docker%20Labs/Lab%2004/images/image-1.png)

### Demo: `--restart always`

#### Step 1: Start a Container with `always`

We will use the image `alpine` for this lab.

```sh
docker run --name neversaydie -it --restart always alpine sh
```

You’ll enter an interactive shell inside an Alpine container.

#### Step 2: Observe Running Processes

Inside the container, run:

```sh
ps -elf
```

**Expected output:**

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/refs/heads/main/Docker%20Labs/Lab%2004/images/image-4.png)

Here:
- `PID 1` is the main process: `sh`
- `ps -elf` is the command you just ran

#### Step 3: Exit the Container

Type `exit` to terminate the `sh` process.

Now, outside the container, run:

```sh
docker ps
```

You’ll see the container is **running again**! Docker restarted it.

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/refs/heads/main/Docker%20Labs/Lab%2004/images/image-5.png)

#### Step 4: Check Restart Count

```sh
docker inspect neversaydie --format '{{.RestartCount}}'
```

**Expected output:**

A number greater than `0` showing how many times it restarted.

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/refs/heads/main/Docker%20Labs/Lab%2004/images/image-6.png)

#### Step 5: Restart Docker Daemon

Try this only if you’re on a system where you can safely restart Docker:

```sh
sudo systemctl restart docker
```

Then run:

```sh
docker ps
```

**Result:** 

Your container `neversaydie` is **still running**! It restarted after the daemon came back up.

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/refs/heads/main/Docker%20Labs/Lab%2004/images/image-7.png)

## Restart Policy: `unless-stopped`

Behaves like `always`, but with one exception:

> If you **manually stop** the container, Docker **won’t restart** it when the daemon restarts.

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/refs/heads/main/Docker%20Labs/Lab%2004/images/image-2.png)

### Demo: `--restart unless-stopped`

#### Step 1: Run Two Containers

```sh
docker run -d --name always --restart always alpine sleep 1d
docker run -d --name unless-stopped --restart unless-stopped alpine sleep 1d
```

#### Step 2: Check They’re Running

```sh
docker ps
```

**Expected output:**

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/refs/heads/main/Docker%20Labs/Lab%2004/images/image-8.png)

#### Step 3: Stop Both

```sh
docker stop always unless-stopped
```

**Verify:**

```sh
docker ps -a
```

Both should show `Exited`.

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/refs/heads/main/Docker%20Labs/Lab%2004/images/image-9.png)

#### Step 4: Restart Docker

```sh
sudo systemctl restart docker
```

#### Step 5: Check What Came Back

```sh
docker ps -a
```

**Expected output:**

- `always` → **Running again**
- `unless-stopped` → **Still Exited**

Docker remembered that you manually stopped the `unless-stopped` container and respected your decision.

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/refs/heads/main/Docker%20Labs/Lab%2004/images/image-10.png)

## Restart Policy: `on-failure`

This policy only restarts the container if the process **fails** (i.e., exits with a non-zero status).

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/refs/heads/main/Docker%20Labs/Lab%2004/images/image-3.png)

### Demo: `--restart on-failure`

#### Step 1: Start a Container

```sh
docker run -d --name on-failure --restart on-failure alpine sleep 1d
```

#### Step 2: Verify the Policy

```sh
docker inspect on-failure --format '{{.HostConfig.RestartPolicy}}'
```

**Expected output:**

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/refs/heads/main/Docker%20Labs/Lab%2004/images/image-11.png)

You can stop the container and restart the daemon to see the container not restarting.

```sh
docker stop on-failure
sudo systemctl restart docker
docker ps -a
```

You can see the container is not restarted because it stopped manually and not because of a failure.

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/refs/heads/main/Docker%20Labs/Lab%2004/images/image-12.png)

> You can test failure behavior by running a command that exits with a non-zero code:
>
> ```sh
> docker run --name check-failure --restart on-failure alpine sh -c "exit 1"
> ```

Observe how Docker retries to restart it. You can check this by running:

```sh
docker ps -a
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/refs/heads/main/Docker%20Labs/Lab%2004/images/image-13.png)

## Conclusion

In this lab, you’ve:

- Explored the **three core Docker restart policies**
- Understood their **behavioral differences**
- Practically tested how they react to crashes and daemon restarts

Restart policies give you a **lightweight self-healing mechanism** without needing external orchestrators. Use them to boost resilience in standalone containers or even as part of more complex deployments.
